04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The walk back to the hotel took longer than Emma expected. She stopped beside the river and looked at the grey water, trying to remember the first time she had heard Claire Morrison's name. In 2011, a disappearance had seemed like a story with a single hidden answer. Now the investigation was made of ordinary details: a form, a date, a person who had signed something, a payment that might or might not have reached its destination.

Back at her hotel, Emma reopened Calum's documents. The trust's message said payment was being processed. It did not say that the college had received it. She had understood the difference intellectually; now it seemed central.

She asked Calum to authorise the college to check its archived finance records. She checked the college's published procedure for historical finance enquiries. It required written authorisation from the former student, and it warned that older records might have been archived or lawfully destroyed. Emma could not make the absence of a document mean more than it did. If the college had no record, she would need to know whether that was unusual before drawing any conclusion.

She drafted a separate request to the foundation for its scholarship conditions and the process by which payments were approved, instructed and confirmed. She did not disclose Fiona's name.

Malcolm Vale remained chairman according to the website. His photograph appeared beside a statement about integrity. Emma closed the page. A chairman's title was not evidence that he had personally authorised any particular transaction.

Sarah rang after nine.

"Any revelation?"

"A date I can check. That's better."

"And the letter?"

"Still private. I don't know who sent it."

After the call, she reread her original article about Claire. There was a paragraph she had once considered powerful: a description of the young woman's silence, followed by the suggestion that she had deliberately cut herself off from her family. Emma remembered the editor's approving nod. She had not remembered the absence of any source for that inference.

She saved the article beside her new notes, not to punish herself but to keep the mistake visible. The fact that she regretted it now did nothing to correct the public record.

Emma made two columns in her notes: verified and unverified. The dates on the correspondence went in the first. The destination of the payments and the identity of whoever had made decisions went in the second. That column was longer.

A message from Calum confirmed that the college had acknowledged his consent form. It had not yet checked the old records. Emma resisted treating the acknowledgement as confirmation of his account.

Another email appeared, this time from Fiona.

Check the original ledger entry dated 19 November 2010. If it differs from the later summary, ask who amended the record. I cannot discuss it further tonight.

Emma read the words twice. Fiona had not alleged theft. She had not named Malcolm or Claire. She had given Emma a testable lead.

Emma wrote one last line in her notebook: 19 November 2010. Original entry. Who changed what—and when?
